title: You Think Kids Need Rewards to Learn, Yet Your Brain Copies What It Sees With Zero Prize
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Albert Bandura (1961): Stanford Nursery Bobo Doll Experiment & Observational Social Learning, grounded in Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross, Sheila A. Ross (1961) (The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that in 1961 at Stanford University Nursery School, Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross, and Sheila Ross tested 72 children aged 3 to 5 years (mean age 52 months), pre-matched for baseline aggressiveness.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: Children were assigned individually to one of three conditions: watching an adult attack a 5-foot inflatable Bobo doll for 10 minutes, watching an adult quietly assemble Tinkertoys for 10 minutes, or no adult model.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross, Sheila A. Ross (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0045925
- Albert Bandura (2021). Influence of Models' Reinforcement Contingencies on the Acquisition of Imitative Responses. Psychological Modeling. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003110156-5
- Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross, Sheila Ross (2019). Imitation of Film-Mediated Aggressive Models (1963). Crime and Media. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780367809195-35

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
